design_detail: Secondary analysis of pooled public-use files of four annual cross-sectional US National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse (NHSDA), 1995–1998 (aggregate sample 86,021, people aged 12 and over; participation 77% to 81% by year). Respondents who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months (age at first use equal to current age or one year less) and had used it in the past year were sorted into three groups: 572 who had started cocaine hydrochloride powder and had never used crack (the reference group, 'Cocaine HCl'), 190 who had started crack recently, with or without a recent start of powder ('Crack (recent HCl?)'), and 93 who had started crack recently after starting powder 2 or more years earlier ('Crack (past HCl)'). The outcomes were seven self-reported clinical features of DSM-IV cocaine dependence in the past 12 months, analysed one at a time with survey-weighted logistic regression without covariates (Table 2) and jointly in a multivariate-response GLM/GEE model adjusted for sex, age, race, daily alcohol use, daily tobacco smoking, cocaine injection and cumulative days of cocaine use (Table 3). No DSM diagnosis was built from the items. The crack–powder difference is tested statistically.
can_establish: How often people in US households in 1995–1998 who had recently started cocaine reported each of seven clinical features of cocaine dependence in the past year, and how much more often those who had recently started smoking crack reported them than those who had started powder only, without adjustment and after adjustment for demographics, daily alcohol and tobacco use, injection and number of days of cocaine use.
cannot_establish: That smoking crack causes these features (one cross-sectional interview, no measure of susceptibility before first use, which the authors say they cannot rule out); the size of a crack effect independent of the amount used (days of use may be a consequence of dependence, and the estimate moves from about 2.3–3.7 without that term to 1.6–1.9 with it); a rate of DSM cocaine dependence (only single features were analysed); the effect of route as such (the route of powder use was not asked, apart from ever injecting); anything about people outside the sampled dwellings, such as homeless people not in shelters; or present-day figures (1995–1998 data, DSM-IV items).

sample.recruitment: Community household survey: NHSDA public-use files for 1995–1998, nationally representative multistage area probability samples of dwelling units and individuals aged 12 and over, aggregate 86,021 respondents, participation 77% to 81% by year; no restriction beyond the onset rules (p. 79, Materials and methods › Participants, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 5th paragraph). Assessment methods were constant over these years; later surveys changed them and were not used (pp. 79–80).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recent start of powder: cocaine hydrochloride powder used in the year before assessment, and age at first powder use equal to the age at assessment or one year less; the same rule for crack. Group Cocaine HCl: recent powder start, never crack (572). Group Crack (recent HCl?): recent crack start; the data cannot separate those who also began powder recently from those who never used powder (190). Group Crack (past HCl): recent crack start with powder begun 2 or more years before assessment, added for comparison (93) (p. 80, Assessment, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Unweighted (Table 1, p. 81): 394 of 855 (46.1%) aged 12–17 (Crack (recent HCl?) 60.0%, Crack (past HCl) 20.4%, Cocaine HCl about 46%, its cell misprinted, see reporting issues); 49.1% female; 58.1% non-Hispanic white; 71.7% had ever smoked tobacco daily; 7.5% drank alcohol daily in the past year; 22 (2.6%) had ever injected cocaine. Weighted to the US population, recent-onset cocaine use was 60:40 male to female, 32:68 younger to older, and 81:19 non-Hispanic white to others (p. 81, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). Item non-response is small: daily smoking missing for 3, injection for 13 and days of cocaine use for 1 of 855 (Table 1, p. 81); how missing covariates were handled in the models is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Household and shelter dwelling units only: people outside the rostered units, such as homeless people not in shelters, are missed, and the authors argue this would make the observed crack excess an underestimate (p. 84, Discussion, 2nd paragraph). Weights adjust for unequal selection and for household and individual non-response (p. 80), but not for unwillingness to report illicit use. The onset rule selects early, mostly light use (45.7% had used cocaine on 1–2 days only), and the Crack (past HCl) group is not a recent start of cocaine at all: its members had used powder for 2 or more years. The crack groups differ from the powder-only group in age (60% vs about 46% adolescents in Crack (recent HCl?); 20% in Crack (past HCl)) and in days of use.

exposure.measurement: Self-administered answer sheets (a small number of respondents had the interviewer read the questions and mark the answers) with standardized NHSDA questions on age at first use and cumulative days of use for all forms of cocaine, a small subset asked separately about crack; daily alcohol use, daily tobacco smoking and ever injecting cocaine also self-reported (p. 80, Assessment, 1st–3rd paragraphs). No biological verification; the authors note that bioassays cannot cover a 0–23-month window (p. 84, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure is the form of cocaine started within the window: cocaine hydrochloride powder only, or crack (smoked). The route of powder use was not asked; the authors treat powder use as nasal insufflation, and injection was recorded only as ever having used a needle to inject cocaine (3 of 572 in Cocaine HCl, 7 of 190 in Crack (recent HCl?), 12 of 93 in Crack (past HCl)). Days of cocaine use, all forms, unweighted (Table 1, p. 81): 1–2 days 53.3% in Cocaine HCl and 12.9% in Crack (past HCl); 101 or more days 2.8% and 32.3%; for Crack (recent HCl?) the printed percentages are 39.0, 32.1, 17.9 and 11.1 for 1–2, 3–11, 12–100 and 101+ days (the counts printed beside them are wrong, see reporting issues). Days of crack use in the two crack groups: 1–2 days 58.4% and 50.5%; 101+ days 7.4% and 11.9%. Amounts and purity were not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Daily tobacco smoking (ever) and daily alcohol use (past year) were measured and adjusted for in Table 3; use of cannabis or any other drug is neither reported nor adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: everyone had used cocaine in the past year, and the features refer to the past 12 months.

comparison.controls: Respondents in the same surveys who had recently started cocaine hydrochloride powder and had never used crack (n=572).
comparison.matching: None. Table 2 estimates are unadjusted (survey-weighted logistic regression, one feature at a time). Table 3 adjusts for sex, age, race (non-Hispanic white vs others), daily alcohol use, daily tobacco smoking, cocaine injection and cumulative days of cocaine use. A model without days of use and an analysis restricted to the 833 respondents who had not injected are described in the text without tables (p. 83).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of susceptibility before first use (psychiatric or family history, impulsivity, social circumstances, other drug use). The authors state that a greater initial susceptibility among people who start with crack cannot be ruled out (abstract, p. 78; Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 84).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls had all used cocaine (powder); 69.2% had ever smoked tobacco daily and 6.5% drank daily (Table 1); other drugs not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Seven standardized NHSDA self-report items on clinical features of DSM-IV cocaine dependence in the past 12 months, asked about any form of cocaine: health problems attributed to the drug; reduced important activities (work, school, childcare, recreation); tolerance; emotional or psychological problems attributed to the drug; salience (a month or more spending a great deal of time getting, using or recovering from the drug); using more than intended; inability to cut down (Fig. 1 legend, p. 82). Respondents were not asked to attribute problems to powder or crack (p. 80, Assessment, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite supportive evidence on the validity and reliability of self-reports in carefully conducted surveys but call the seven-item NHSDA assessment much less comprehensive than the UM-CIDI of the National Comorbidity Survey and are cautious about a dependence 'diagnosis' from it (p. 84, Discussion, 3rd paragraph). No withdrawal item is among the seven.
outcomes.operationalization: Each feature coded present or absent; by choice, no count and no DSM diagnosis were built (p. 80, Assessment, 6th paragraph). 'Risk' is the weighted cumulative occurrence of a feature in the past year among people whose cocaine use began 0–23 months before (Fig. 1); the 'relative risks' of Tables 2 and 3 are odds ratios (p. 80, Data analysis, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 footnote a).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the 14 feature-by-group contrasts of Table 2 (7 features by 2 crack groups). The multivariate GEE model of Table 3 summarizes across features with one crack estimate per group.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-administered; the authors state that neither interviewers nor respondents knew that crack-associated risk would be studied (p. 84, Discussion, 4th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Weighted cumulative occurrence in the past year (Fig. 1, p. 82; no values printed, read by the editors from the bar heights, approximate): Cocaine HCl about 5–12% for every feature (reduced activities 5.2%, tolerance 5.9%, health problems 6.6%, emotional problems 10.1%, salience 10.1%, inability to cut down 10.4%, more than intended 12.2%); Crack (recent HCl?) about 18–32%; Crack (past HCl) about 11–33%. Unadjusted survey-weighted odds ratios labelled relative risks (Table 2, p. 83), Crack (recent HCl?) vs Cocaine HCl: health problems 3.0 (0.9–9.7), P=0.06; reduced activities 5.6 (1.9–15.9); tolerance 4.8 (1.8–12.6); emotional problems 3.5 (1.6–7.7); salience 3.4 (1.5–7.7); more than intended 3.1 (1.4–7.0); inability to cut down 4.0 (1.9–8.7); P<0.01 for each of these six. Crack (past HCl) vs Cocaine HCl: health problems 2.7 (1.0–7.2), P=0.05; reduced activities 2.3 (0.9–6.4), P=0.10; tolerance 2.7 (1.2–6.2), P=0.02; emotional problems 2.0 (0.9–4.5), P=0.08; salience 4.4 (2.0–9.5), P<0.01; more than intended 2.4 (1.0–5.7), P=0.04; inability to cut down 1.6 (0.6–4.2), P=0.30. Adjusted GEE odds ratio across all seven features (Table 3, p. 83): Crack (recent HCl?) 1.9 (1.4–2.5), P<0.01; Crack (past HCl) 1.6 (1.0–2.5), P=0.04; without the cumulative-days term about 2.3–3.7 (P<0.001; no intervals, no table; p. 83). Editors' calculation: the Table 2 odds ratios are reproduced, within the error of reading Fig. 1, from the Fig. 1 percentages, which confirms they are unadjusted weighted odds ratios; the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 1.5–4.4 rather than 1.6–5.6 (for example tolerance 23.0% vs 5.9%, prevalence ratio about 3.9 against the printed 4.8).
analysis.covariates: Table 2: none. Table 3: sex, age, race (non-Hispanic white vs others), daily alcohol use in the past year, ever daily tobacco smoking, ever injecting cocaine, cumulative days of cocaine use (Table 3 footnote d, p. 83). Whether survey weights were applied in the GEE model is not stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: The feature-specific crack estimates from the re-specified model with 12 product terms (pp. 80–81) are not reported, although the abstract says the crack excess is more prominent for tolerance and narrowed behavioural repertoire. The model without days of use is reported only as a range (about 2.3–3.7) without intervals, and the restriction to 833 people who had not injected only as showing no appreciable change (p. 83). The six feature rows of Table 3 are odds of reporting each feature relative to health problems (the reference feature), not crack–powder contrasts, and are easily misread as such.
analysis.power: Not reported. The crack groups are small (190 and 93; 13 to 49 people reporting each feature in Table 2), giving wide intervals (for example 1.9–15.9).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people in US households who had started cocaine in the previous 0–23 months (1995–1998), those who had started smoking crack reported each of seven dependence features roughly 2 to 4 times as often as those who had started powder only (weighted past-year occurrence about 18–32% and 11–33% against 5–12%). After adjustment that included cumulative days of cocaine use, the summary odds ratio across features was 1.9 (1.4–2.5) for a recent start of crack and 1.6 (1.0–2.5) for crack begun after 2 or more years of powder use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says most features occurred 2–3 times more often among people smoking crack "even with statistical adjustment for frequency of cocaine use (P<0.01)" (p. 78); the only adjusted estimates reported that include days of use are 1.6 (P=0.04) and 1.9 (P<0.01) (Table 3, p. 83), and the larger range of about 2.3–3.7 comes from the model without days of use (p. 83). The abstract's statement that the excess is more prominent for tolerance and narrowed behavioural repertoire rests on unadjusted point estimates with overlapping intervals (Table 2), not on the feature-specific model, whose results are not shown; narrowed repertoire (reduced activities) was not significant for Crack (past HCl) (P=0.10). Odds ratios are called relative risks throughout although the features occurred in 11–33% of the crack groups, so the odds ratios overstate the prevalence ratios (editors' calculation, about 1.5–4.4 against 1.6–5.6). The title and summary speak of the risk of becoming dependent, but no dependence diagnosis was made, nearly half the sample had used on 1–2 days only, and 'risk' is a cross-sectional proportion. Against this, the conclusion is hedged: crack smoking may increase risk, and the authors say they cannot rule out a greater initial susceptibility (abstract, p. 78; Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 84). The summary paragraph says years where months are meant (p. 85).

timeline.event: National Comorbidity Survey estimates of dependence among people who had used cocaine, cited here as background (about 1 in 6 eventually dependent; 5–6% within 1–2 years of starting, with Wagner and Anthony, 2002)

Narrative review of crack and cocaine hydrochloride concluding that smoked use carries more severe dependence than intranasal use, drawing on treatment, jail, street and laboratory samples; Chen and Anthony call their findings consistent with it (p. 84)
Chen and Kandel, NHSDA analysis: crack smoking associated with being an active case of cocaine dependence among all recently active people who used cocaine (as described here, p. 84; not read)
Systematic review of health outcomes of crack use includes this study among 12 comparing crack with other cocaine use and calls that evidence on dependence, anxiety and depression mixed; not pooled

replication.where_it_stands: In the sources read for this round, this is the only population-based estimate of a crack-associated excess in early dependence features restricted to people who had just started cocaine; no direct replication has been read. Its direction agrees with the treatment- and laboratory-based evidence summarized by Hatsukami and Fischman (1996), but the one later systematic synthesis read (Butler et al., 2017) describes comparisons of crack with other cocaine use on dependence as mixed and pools none of them. Whether crack itself, the amount used, or pre-existing susceptibility explains the excess remains open.

funding.funder: Supported via NIDA DA09897 and its 'transitions research supplement', NIDA DA008199, and the NHSDA research groups at SAMHSA and RTI (Acknowledgements, p. 85).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, and the Department of Epidemiology, Michigan State University. The data are from the federal survey run by SAMHSA, whose NHSDA research groups (with RTI) are named among the supporters. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people sampled before or at first cocaine use, with susceptibility measured at baseline (psychiatric and family history, impulsivity, social circumstances, other drug use), repeated measurement of form, route and frequency of use, and dependence assessed by a full diagnostic interview, analysing time to dependence by form of first use with frequency treated as a possible mediator rather than only as a confounder; or the case-crossover design the authors suggest to address individual susceptibility (p. 84).

domains.note: Table 2 is unadjusted. Table 3 adjusts for demographics, daily alcohol and tobacco use, injection and days of use, but not for other drug use, psychiatric or family history, social circumstances or pre-use susceptibility, which the authors say cannot be ruled out. Days of use may be partly a consequence of dependence, so adjusting for it may remove part of a real crack effect, while leaving it out leaves confounding by amount used.

Self-reported form and age at first use; the onset window is defined from ages in whole years (0–23 months); Crack (recent HCl?) mixes people with and without a recent start of powder; the route of powder use was assumed (nasal), only ever injecting was asked.

domains.domain: Selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Household and shelter sample with 77–81% participation; homeless people outside shelters are missed; the onset rule selects early, mostly light use; Crack (past HCl) consists of people with 2 or more years of powder use compared with new starters.
Treatment after starting cocaine was not measured, but is unlikely to have mattered within 0–23 months of onset.
At most 13 of 855 values missing for any covariate (Table 1); handling not stated.

Seven self-report items, two of which require attributing health or emotional problems to the drug; respondents did not know the hypothesis (authors' statement), but people who smoke crack may attribute problems to cocaine differently; the 12-month window is longer than the time since onset for some respondents.

Results of the feature-specific model with 12 product terms are not shown; the model without days of use is given only as a range without intervals; the injection-restricted analysis is not shown; the abstract's adjusted 2–3-fold statement cannot be traced to a reported result.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used for the card because the claims it will support are associations between the form of cocaine started and dependence features. The association is consistent across features and survives adjustment for demographics, alcohol, tobacco, injection and days of use, but it rests on self-report in a single cross-sectional interview and cannot be separated from pre-existing susceptibility or from the amount used, which may itself lie on the causal path; for any causal reading the risk of bias is high. The JBI prevalence checklist was applied to the cumulative-occurrence figures (Fig. 1), editors' summary moderate risk: 1 sample frame partial-yes (households and shelters only); 2 sampling yes (multistage probability, weighted); 3 sample size partial-yes (adequate for Cocaine HCl, small crack groups of 190 and 93); 4 subjects and setting yes (unweighted Table 1 plus weighted ratios); 5 coverage of the identified sample yes (non-response weights); 6 valid identification of the condition partial-yes (seven self-report items, not a diagnosis); 7 standard measurement yes (items constant over 1995–1998); 8 statistical analysis partial-yes (weighted estimates, but Fig. 1 prints no values or intervals); 9 response rate yes (77–81%). The source may be cited for the size of the crack-associated excess in reported dependence features among people in US households who had just started cocaine in 1995–1998, unadjusted and adjusted, as an association; not for a causal effect of smoking crack, for a rate of dependence, or for present-day populations.

key_findings.finding: 855 respondents to the 1995–1998 NHSDA (aggregate sample 86,021; participation 77% to 81% by year) had started cocaine within roughly 0–23 months: 572 had started powder and never used crack, 190 had started crack (with or without a recent start of powder), and 93 had started crack after powder use begun 2 or more years earlier.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods (p. 78); Materials and methods › Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 79); Assessment, 4th paragraph (p. 80); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 81)

key_findings.finding: Unweighted sample: 46.1% aged 12–17, 49.1% female, 58.1% non-Hispanic white; 45.7% had used cocaine on 1–2 days only; 71.7% (613) had ever smoked tobacco daily, 7.5% (64) drank daily in the past year, and 22 (2.6%) had ever injected cocaine. Weighted, the US recent-onset population was 60:40 male to female, 32:68 younger to older and 81:19 non-Hispanic white to others.
key_findings.note: The text gives daily drinking as roughly 8% (n=64); Table 1 gives 7.5%.

key_findings.finding: Weighted past-year occurrence of each dependence feature was about 5–12% among people who had started powder only; for example narrowed repertoire (reduced important activities) roughly 5% against 20–25% in Crack (recent HCl?), and salience roughly 10% against 28–34% in the crack groups. Editors' reading of Fig. 1 for all seven features: about 18–32% in Crack (recent HCl?) and about 11–33% in Crack (past HCl).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 78); Results, 3rd paragraph and Fig. 1 (p. 82)
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 prints no values. The 5–12%, 20–25% and 28–34% figures are the authors'; the group ranges 18–32% and 11–33% and the single values are the editors' reading of bar heights at 300 dpi (Cocaine HCl: reduced activities 5.2, tolerance 5.9, health problems 6.6, emotional problems 10.1, salience 10.1, inability to cut down 10.4, more than intended 12.2; Crack (recent HCl?) 17.7–31.8; Crack (past HCl) 11.1–33.2), approximate to about 0.3 points.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted survey-weighted odds ratios (labelled relative risks), Crack (recent HCl?) vs Cocaine HCl: health problems 3.0 (0.9–9.7), P=0.06; reduced activities 5.6 (1.9–15.9); tolerance 4.8 (1.8–12.6); emotional problems 3.5 (1.6–7.7); salience 3.4 (1.5–7.7); more than intended 3.1 (1.4–7.0); inability to cut down 4.0 (1.9–8.7); P<0.01 for each of the last six.
key_findings.note: No covariates; numbers reporting each feature are small (22–49 of 190).

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted survey-weighted odds ratios, Crack (past HCl) vs Cocaine HCl: health problems 2.7 (1.0–7.2), P=0.05; reduced activities 2.3 (0.9–6.4), P=0.10; tolerance 2.7 (1.2–6.2), P=0.02; emotional problems 2.0 (0.9–4.5), P=0.08; salience 4.4 (2.0–9.5), P<0.01; more than intended 2.4 (1.0–5.7), P=0.04; inability to cut down 1.6 (0.6–4.2), P=0.30.
key_findings.note: This group had used powder for 2 or more years, so the contrast is not between new starters.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for sex, age, race, daily alcohol use, daily tobacco smoking, cocaine injection and cumulative days of cocaine use, the multivariate GEE odds ratio across all seven features, against people who had started powder only, was 1.9 (1.4–2.5), P<0.01, for Crack (recent HCl?) and 1.6 (1.0–2.5), P=0.04, for Crack (past HCl).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 82, continuing on p. 83); Table 3, rows under 'Estimated effect of the form'

key_findings.finding: Without the cumulative-days term, the crack-associated estimate was about 2.3–3.7 (P<0.001), reported without intervals or a table; restricting the analysis to the 833 respondents who had not injected changed the estimates little (not shown).

The six feature rows of Table 3 (for example salience 2.6, 2.0–3.4; reduced activities 1.2, 0.9–1.6) are the adjusted odds of reporting each feature relative to health problems, the reference feature, across all 855 respondents; they are not crack–powder contrasts.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, upper rows and footnote b

key_findings.finding: The 'relative risks' of Tables 2 and 3 are odds ratios, as the Methods and the Table 2 footnote state. Editors' calculation from the Fig. 1 readings: the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 1.5–4.4 (for example tolerance about 3.9 in Crack (recent HCl?) against the printed 4.8).
key_findings.locator: Data analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 80); Fig. 1 (p. 82); Table 2 footnote a (p. 83)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that no one has ruled out that people who start with crack are more susceptible to dependence from the outset, that the seven-item NHSDA assessment is much less comprehensive than a full diagnostic interview, that bioassays were not used, and that household sampling misses homeless people outside shelters, which they expect to make the crack excess an underestimate.

The authors speculate, and say so, that the influence of smoked crack on dependence may be most salient when crack smoking starts in the first 0–23 months of cocaine use, so that studies of treatment seekers or people with long cocaine histories could underestimate it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the Cocaine HCl age 12–17 cell as 361 (46.6%) beside 311 (54.4%) aged 18 and over in a group of 572. Editors' arithmetic: 361 + 311 = 672, not 572; the total row (394 = x + 114 + 19) and the 54.4% imply 261 (45.6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the adolescent share of the powder-only group is about 46%.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the counts printed for days of cocaine use (all forms) in the Crack (recent HCl?) column (111, 48, 17, 14) repeat that column's counts for days of crack use, while the percentages printed beside them are 39.0, 32.1, 17.9 and 11.1. Editors' arithmetic: those percentages of 190, and the row totals less the other two columns, both give 74, 61, 34 and 21.
reporting_issues.consequence: This group's days-of-use distribution must be taken from the percentages; the printed counts understate its heavier use (101 or more days: 21 people, not 14).

reporting_issues.issue: Minor percentage slips in Table 1: 239 with no daily smoking printed as 28.3%, 76 of 93 as 81.1%, 11 of 93 as 11.9%, and 67 of 855 as 8.0%. Editors' arithmetic: 28.0%, 81.7%, 11.8% and 7.8%.

The abstract states that most features occurred 2–3 times more often with crack even with adjustment for frequency of use (P<0.01); the adjusted estimates that include days of use are 1.6 (P=0.04) and 1.9 (P<0.01), and 2.3–3.7 is the estimate without that term.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must give 1.6–1.9 as the estimate adjusted for days of use and describe 2.3–3.7 as not adjusted for it.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Relative risk' (Tables 2 and 3 and the text) labels odds ratios (Methods, p. 80; Table 2 footnote a). Editors' reading of Fig. 1: the features were present in about 11–33% of the crack groups, so the odds ratios exceed the prevalence ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should call them odds ratios; prevalence ratios from Fig. 1 are about 1.5–4.4 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The re-specified model with 12 product terms that estimates a separate crack relationship for each feature (pp. 80–81) has no reported results, yet the abstract names the features for which the excess is more prominent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Feature-specific differences can be cited only as unadjusted Table 2 estimates with overlapping intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 is headed with all 855 respondents and the abstract frames the study as risk within 1–2 years of starting cocaine, but the Crack (past HCl) group had started powder 2 or more years before assessment.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the Crack (recent HCl?) contrast concerns people who had just started cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary paragraph speaks of the first 0–23 years after onset of cocaine use, where 0–23 months is meant everywhere else.
